title: The Security Deposit Standoff
background: Maya rented a one-bedroom apartment from Evan for 18 months. After moving out, Evan withheld most of her security deposit for cleaning and carpet repairs. Maya demands a full refund; Evan insists the deductions are justified.
facts: Maya moved out on March 1.
Evan withheld $1,200 of the $1,500 security deposit for cleaning and carpet replacement.
Maya left the carpet with three large wine stains and scuff marks on the walls.
Evan had promised in February to replace the aging carpet before Maya's lease ended, but never did.
Maya made a late rent payment in September; Evan sent a written warning about it.
Evan hired a professional cleaning service for $400 after Maya moved out.
Maya gave Evan her new mailing address on March 2.
Evan mailed the itemized deduction list to the old apartment address on April 15, which was 12 days after the legal deadline.
The lease required Maya to return the apartment 'broom-clean and damage-free.'
Maya declined Evan's request for a pre-move-out walkthrough.
dispute: Maya wants the full $1,500 deposit returned, arguing the deductions were untimely, sent to the wrong address, and that Evan had already planned to replace the carpet. Evan wants to keep the $1,200, arguing the unit was left damaged and the cleaning cost was legitimate.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses: late rent payment, left wine stains and scuffs, refused walkthrough, didn't professionally clean; Evan's lapses: missed the itemized-list deadline, sent it to the wrong address, broke his promise to replace the carpet, and the cleaning charge was arguably inflated for the actual work done.

title: The Two-Week Sink Repair and the $50 Communication Fee
background: Maya rents an apartment from David. In early June, her kitchen sink began leaking and the cabinet warped. David arranged a repair that took nearly a month to complete, and afterwards charged Maya a $50 fee for what he called 'extra communication handling.'
facts: On June 1, Maya emailed David: "The kitchen sink is leaking and the cabinet is warping."
On June 3, David replied: "I'll send a plumber next week."
On June 10, no plumber had arrived; Maya sent a second email.
On June 11, David replied: "Plumber is scheduled for June 15."
On June 15, the plumber inspected the sink and said the needed part was not in stock and that he would order it.
On June 20, Maya texted David: "This is getting ridiculous, I expect action this week."
On June 22, David ordered the part online after learning the plumber had not ordered it.
On June 25, Maya sent a formal complaint to the property management company without informing David.
The part arrived on June 28; the plumber fixed the sink on July 1.
On July 2, David sent Maya an invoice for $50 for 'extra communication handling.'
dispute: Maya wants David to waive the $50 fee and apologize for the delay. David wants Maya to pay the $50 and acknowledge that her unilateral complaint to management was unfair.
fault_rationale: David missed his own promised timeline and failed to verify the plumber's order, while Maya sent a snide text and escalated to management without prior notice—each has a concrete lapse.

title: The Lease-Break Fee Dispute
background: Mark rented an apartment to Lisa under a one-year lease, which included an explicit early termination clause.
facts: On January 1, 2025, Mark and Lisa signed a 12-month lease for apartment 4B starting February 1, 2025, with monthly rent of $1200.
The lease states that early termination requires 60 days' notice and payment of a $2000 lease-break fee.
On June 15, 2025, Lisa informed Mark in writing that she would move out on July 1, 2025.
Lisa moved out on July 5, 2025, leaving without paying rent for August.
Mark inspected the apartment and found it undamaged but slightly dusty.
Mark listed the apartment on August 1, 2025, and found a new tenant who moved in on September 1, 2025.
Mark sent Lisa a bill for the $2000 lease-break fee on August 10, 2025.
Lisa responded that she lost her job and had to move to a cheaper city.
Lisa offered to pay $500 as a 'goodwill' fee.
Mark refused the offer and demanded the full $2000 per the lease.
dispute: Mark wants the full $2000 lease-break fee as stated in the lease; Lisa wants to pay only $500 due to financial hardship.
fault_rationale: Lisa clearly violated the lease by moving out early without the required notice and refusing to pay the contractual fee, while Mark followed the lease terms and made reasonable efforts to re-rent the property.
